summaries.summary: Privacy policies disclose company data practices under notice and choice, but legitimacy depends on users reading and understanding them, which seldom occurs.
Ubiquitous monitoring and data misuse scandals motivate privacy as an NLP domain where identifying salient issues could have real-world impact.
The paragraph lists two Google Play app URLs and notes that a question might lack supporting evidence in the privacy policy.
The authors contribute PrivacyQA, a corpus of 1750 privacy-policy questions and over 3500 expert annotations, to support question-answering methods.
Prior privacy-policy NLP work is reviewed, and PrivacyQA is contrasted with PolisisQA as larger, expert-answered, and more diverse.
The work relates to open-domain reading comprehension and legal NLP, noting privacy policies target the general public despite differing writer goals.
PrivacyQA collects English privacy policies from 35 mobile applications across Google Play Store categories, balancing around 5 million installs before April 1, 2018.
Crowdworkers elicit privacy-policy questions without seeing policies, to avoid biases and encourage varied questions beyond described practices.
Crowdworkers see Google Play Store app information, imagine a trusted privacy assistant, and provide five questions per app for $2.
Seven legally trained experts answer Turker questions by identifying evidence and annotating relevance, subjectivity, OPP-115 category, and answer likelihood.
PrivacyQA contains 1750 questions over 35 mobile applications, with 1350 training questions over 27 apps and 400 test questions over 8 documents.
PrivacyQA questions show low redundancy, average 8.4 words, policies average ~3000 words, and answers typically have ~100 words of evidence.
Questions are organized under nine categories from the OPP-115 Corpus annotation scheme.
First Party Collection/Use covers what, why and how information is collected by the service provider.
Third Party Sharing/Collection covers what, why and how information is shared with or collected by third parties.
Data Security covers protection measures for user information.
Data Retention covers how long user information will be stored.
User Choice/Control covers control options available to users.
User Access, Edit and Deletion covers if and how users can access, edit or delete information.
Policy Change covers informing users if policy information has been changed.
International and Specific Audiences covers practices pertaining to a specific group of users.
Other covers general text, contact information or practices not covered by other categories.
Experts assign OPP-115 categories, with agreement rules described, and first party and third party questions form nearly 66.4% of all questions.
The authors analyze expert disagreement using 100 sampled test instances, defining disagreement as no overlap between experts' relevant text.
Experts agree on answers for 74% of questions and disagree on 26%, with causes including question intent, evidence, policy content, partial answers, and subjectivity.
The experiments evaluate machine learning methods for identifying relevant evidence, answerability baselines, evidence identification, and aspects making questions unanswerable.
Answerability identification is a binary classification task predicting whether a question can be answered in isolation, with three baselines improving over majority-class.
SVM uses SVM-BOW, SVM-BOW + LEN, and SVM-BOW + LEN + POS features, producing 200, 201 and 228 dimensions for a linear-kernel SVM.
CNN uses GloVe word embeddings and a filter size of 5 with 64 filters to encode questions.
BERT-base is fine-tuned on binary answerability identification with learning rate 2e-5 for 3 epochs and maximum sequence length 128.
Privacy question answering is framed as answer sentence selection, identifying evidence sentences from all candidate sentences in each policy.
The evaluation metric is sentence-level F1, measuring overlap between predicted and gold-reference sentences and averaging maximum F1 from each n$-$1 subset.
The authors describe baselines for answer sentence selection, including a human performance baseline.
The No-Answer Baseline (NA) quantifies identifying every question as unanswerable because many questions are difficult to answer from privacy policies.
The Word Count Baseline retrieves top candidate policy sentences by counting shared question words, including the top 2, 3 and 5 candidates.
Two BERT-based baselines classify query-policy sentence pairs for evidence, with Bert + Unanswerable adding a separately trained answerability classifier.
Human Performance computes F1 for each annotator reference against remaining references and averages the maximum F1 across all reference answers.
bert performs best on binary answerability identification, and most baselines exceed majority-class, suggesting questions contain answerability information.
The No-answer (NA) baseline reaches 28 F1, while Bert + Unanswerable achieves 39.8 F1, leaving headroom to human performance.
Error analysis by OPP-115 categories compares the best BERT variant, NA, and human performance, showing room for improvement especially for first party, third party and data retention.
BERT makes 124 answerability mistakes, mostly answerable questions marked unanswerable, with expert judgments suggesting nuanced answerability understanding may help.
Legal experts identify causes of unanswerability, arguing systems may need different treatments for different categories of unanswerable questions.
Incomprehensibility means a question is incomprehensible to the extent that its meaning is not intelligible.
Relevance asks whether a question is in the scope of what could be answered by reading the privacy policy.
Ill-formedness asks whether a question is ambiguous or vague, distinguishing ambiguity from vague concepts with unclear or soft definitions.
Silence means other policies answer this type of question but this one does not.
Atypicality means the question is unlikely for any policy policy to have an answer to the question.
Experts classify all 573 unanswerable questions, reporting 4.18% incomprehensible, 50% likely answerable, 33.1% privacy-related out of scope, and 16.9% completely out-of-scope.
A sample of 100 natural unanswerable questions shows varied error types, including 20% not questions, 12% atypicality-like, and 42% lacking document answers.
PrivacyQA is presented as the first significant corpus of privacy policy questions and more than 3500 expert annotations, with strong neural baselines achieving only 39.8 F1.
This research was supported by National Science Foundation Secure and Trustworthy Computing program grants and a DARPA Brandeis grant, with thanks to named individuals, reviewers, and crowdworkers.
